title: Half of Heaven, Rotting in the Vault
excerpt: Why we forgot more than half of all women artists — and why their worth today is dearer than ever.
content:
The Great Omission

Picture this: you paint your whole life long. You wield a brush so virtuosically that Michelangelo himself takes notice. You run your own studio, you feed your family with it, you shape the aesthetic of a century. And then you vanish. Not because your paintings were bad. Not because they burned. But because the system we call the art market has the memory of a goldfish — and this goldfish hates women.

The numbers are laughable. More than half of all artists were and are women. Yet on the art market they form a minority you have to hunt for with a magnifying glass. LOST WOMAN ART blew the lid off it: a mechanism of systematic forgetting, perfected like Swiss clockwork. We are not talking about coincidence here. We are talking about structure.

The Art of Drawing and Its Chains

In 1780 Angelica Kauffman painted The Art of Design. A self-assured statement, a manifesto in oil. But anyone who looks closely catches the bitter irony: the artist is allowed to embody talent, but not flesh. Access to nude models was denied to her. So instead she painted ideas, allegories, the abstraction of skill — while her male colleagues were free to study naked reality and sell it. An elegant prison of recognition and restriction.

And Kauffman was the lucky one. She had commissions, fame, a name. Others vanished completely. Judith Leyster, who worked alongside Frans Hals in the 17th century and perfected his style so thoroughly that her works were sold under his name for centuries. Amalie Bensinger, lost in the archive. Her paintings exist, but the context has been scrubbed away like a Stalin-era photograph.

  • Sofonisba Anguissola painted her 1557 portrait of her mother Bianca Ponzoni with an intensity that silenced the Spanish court
  • She impressed Michelangelo as a portraitist — today barely anyone knows her outside of footnotes
  • Lavinia Fontana ran her own studio and took commissions from nobility, yet her power portraits are now niche trivia

When Flowers Were Worth More Than Women

Rachel Ruysch was one of the highest-paid artists of the Baroque. Read that again. Highest-paid. Her flower still lifes were so obsessively detailed, so botanically precise, that they verge on hyperreal — a hype she conjured in oil on canvas long before digital cameras existed. She made money, serious money. But the money didn't help. The money didn't save her from the index of oblivion.

Because capitalism and art history are no friends of justice. They are friends of narrative. And the narrative ran: genius is male. Period. The market did reward Ruysch with the flourishing $77 equivalents of her time, but not with eternity. Her paintings hang today wherever they don't get in the way.

The Avant-Garde We Locked Away

And then there is Hilma af Klint. The woman who invented abstraction before Kandinsky had any idea the world could be taken apart into form and color. In 1906, years before the "first" abstract painting in history, she conjured works born of spirituality and visions. Yet she asked that they not be exhibited until decades after her death.

An act of prophetic wisdom or desperate resignation? Probably both. She knew the system couldn't digest her. That the market, ravenous for fresh commodity-images, would have turned her spirituality into speculation. So she hid them. A radical act of resistance: I show you nothing, so you can't devour it.

Berthe Morisot, by contrast, exhibited. Everywhere. She was a founding member of Impressionism, not as a muse, not as a model, but as a creator. Her delicate style shaped Renoir, Manet, the whole gang. Yet in the halls that bear those names today, she hangs only sporadically. As a side dish. As a nice change of pace, going for $77 to $777, depending on how scarce the supply happens to be.

I LAUGH YOU

Now come the rescue missions. Geniale Frauen at the Bucerius Kunst Forum. Künstlerinnen! at the Kunstpalast Düsseldorf. 150 works by 30 women artists, presented as a discovery that isn't one. We celebrate them now, when there is nothing left in it for them. We buy up their fragments according to scarcity, according to whatever was left behind.

But here is the beautiful part: the art itself couldn't care less. Artemisia Gentileschi's Judith goes on slaying her Holofernes, unimpressed by whether the picture is cheap or expensive today. The meaning lives in the detail, in every single fragment of consciousness these women pinned to canvas. They expressed free will exactly where the system wanted them silenced.

And that is why I stand in front of these paintings and laugh. A bitter, furious, loving laugh. I LAUGH YOU, Artemisia. I LAUGH YOU, Hilma. You won. Not because we are finally allowed to buy you, but because you outlived us. Capitalism eats everything, but it didn't digest you. You are the real fragments, the ones holding meaning intact while the rest of us out here wave our price tags around.
